status_reasoning: The behavioral results demonstrate robust sequence-specific learning with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests with pre-test correction). The finding of both general learning (796ms improvement on untrained sequences) and sequence-specific learning (additional 237ms advantage for trained sequences, t(14)=5.749, p<0.0001) is well-supported. Intermanual transfer is also demonstrated with proper statistics, though the effect is smaller (95ms, t(14)=2.802, p=0.014).

The finding of reduced average activity for trained sequences is well-supported by whole-brain analysis with appropriate multiple comparison correction. The result is particularly compelling because trained sequences were executed faster and with higher forces, yet showed less activity in PMd and IPS bilaterally. The absence of any regions showing increased activity for trained sequences strengthens the conclusion that average activity changes do not reflect the neural basis of skill learning.

The demonstration that both trained and untrained sequences can be discriminated using MVPA is well-supported with appropriate cross-validation and statistical testing. Classification accuracies of ~55% (vs. 25% chance) in M1, PMd, and IPS are highly significant after multiple comparison correction. The finding extends beyond previously known areas (M1, SMA) to include parietal and lateral premotor regions, representing a novel contribution. The replicability across subjects strengthens the result.

The central finding that trained sequences show higher classification accuracy than untrained sequences is supported by multiple converging analyses: global average (38.4% vs 34.2%, t(15)=2.203, p=0.022), increased cortical surface area (35.12 to 46.93 cm², t(15)=1.963, p=0.034), and region-specific effects in left SMA/pre-SMA (36% to 46%, p-corrected<0.012). The effect survives correction for behavioral differences (C60-C62), ruling out the alternative explanation that neural differences simply reflect performance differences.

The dimensionality analysis provides strong evidence that sequences are encoded in unique spatial patterns rather than scaled versions of a common pattern. The finding that classification accuracy is highest when using all three spatial components (significant in all ROIs for both trained and untrained sequences, all t(15)>2.496, p<0.025) rules out alternative explanations based on single variables like difficulty or force. This sophisticated analysis strengthens the interpretation of the classification results.

The pattern decomposition analysis demonstrates that training increases the sequence-specific component while the common component (100x larger) follows mean activation. The finding that trained patterns are more evenly distributed than random patterns (significant deviation in S1, M1, PMd, SMA/pre-SMA, and IPS, all t(15)>2.429, p<0.028) supports the hypothesis of specialized neuronal circuits. This provides mechanistic insight beyond simple classification accuracy differences.

While the temporal analysis shows early classification accuracy (S1 at TR2, t(15)=3.335, p=0.002) and sustained representation during execution, the experimental design confounds instruction and execution phases. The authors acknowledge this limitation (C91), and the interpretation that patterns reflect both instruction-related and execution-related activity remains uncertain. Further experiments with separated instruction and execution phases would be needed to definitively determine the contribution of each phase.

The finding of bilateral or left-lateralized learning effects despite training only the left hand is supported by both neural (C108) and behavioral (C110) data. The behavioral intermanual transfer (95ms advantage, t(14)=2.802, p=0.014) provides converging evidence. The interpretation linking this to left hemisphere specialization for complex movements is appropriately supported by citation to prior work (Verstynen et al., 2005).

The mechanistic interpretation that observed patterns reflect sequentially-tuned neurons is plausible and supported by prior single-cell studies (C70), but remains speculative for the current data. The authors appropriately acknowledge multiple alternative explanations (phonological rehearsal, timing vs. order coding, effector-specificity) and note that the exact response characteristics remain unclear (C87). The spatial resolution requirements for fMRI detection (C72) add further uncertainty. Additional experiments are explicitly stated as necessary (C92).

The synthesis explaining how competing mechanisms (increased recruitment vs. increased efficiency) can produce complex average activity changes while MVPA reveals underlying specialization is well-reasoned and supported by the data. The finding that average activity decreased while pattern discriminability increased (C111, C120) directly supports this framework. The conclusion that skill learning generates distributed specialized representations (C122) integrates the behavioral and neural findings coherently and is appropriately supported by citations reconciling prior inconsistent results (C118).
